en.lead_text:
We recommend refraining from using any offensive language and hate speech. The United Nations defines hate speech as "'discriminatory' (biased, bigoted or intolerant) or 'pejorative' (prejudiced, contemptuous or demeaning) of an individual or group."

Using offensive language and hate speech in the workplace...

  • has legal implications.
  • can prompt disciplinary action.
  • contributes to a dehumanizing workplace climate for everyone, including but not limited to victims, witnesses, and bystanders.
  • may cause lasting damage to your career and professional standing.

en.lead_text:
Cognitive biases generally apply to how our brain uses data, while implicit biases color how we use that data through the lens of an individual’s personal characteristics. Both types of bias—cognitive and implicit—reflect the mind’s inappropriate application of shortcuts to newly available information, leading to assumptions and conclusions that do not truly fit the data at hand.  (Comp. this source).


Cognitive bias is caused by the tendency of the human brain to simplify information processing through a filter of personal experience and preferences. The filtering process is a coping mechanism that enables the brain to prioritize and process large amounts of information quickly.

Examples

  • Confirmation bias - we are drawn to details that confirm our own beliefs.
  • Stereotypical bias - we discard specifics to form generalities.
  • Identifiable victim bias - to stay focused, we favor the immediate, relatable thing in front of us.

Implicit bias describes when we have attitudes towards people or associate stereotypes with them without our conscious knowledge. Research suggests that people can act on the basis of prejudice and stereotypes without intending to do so, and these actions can be in direct contradiction to a person's espoused beliefs and values. We all have implicit biases, even if we do not act on them—they shape how we perceive people, their actions, and characteristics.

Examples

  • Bob or Rashid? Being more receptive to familiar-sounding names.
  • A 50-year old programmer? Assuming people age out of a innovation-driven field.
  • Beauty or brains? Assuming looks are unlikely to coincide with intelligence and skills.
